evidence: Caes. BG 1.1: quī ipsōrum linguā Celtae, nostrā Gallī appellantur
Cic. Fin. 1.10: Latīnam linguam nōn modo nōn inopem … sed locuplētiōrem etiam esse quam Graecam
terms.comment: Utraque lingua, both languages: for a Roman, Greek and Latin (Hor. S. 1.10.23; Quint. 1.1.14).

terms.gloss: language, the speech of a people
evidence: Quint. 1.1.12: ā sermōne Graecō puerum incipere mālō
Cic. de Or. 3.42 (Lewis & Short): in Latīnō sermōne
terms.comment: Sermō Latīnus, the Latin language; also talk, conversation (see talk).
In late antiquity a turn of phrase peculiar to a language (Charisius); a language only in medieval and later Latin (Dante, Marco Polo, in Morgan–Owens). Classical prose says lingua or sermō.

phrases.latin: tertiam quī ipsōrum linguā Celtae, nostrā Gallī appellantur
phrases.english: the third by those who are called Celts in their own language, Gauls in ours

phrases.latin: ita fīet, ut, cum aequālī cūrā linguam utramque tuērī coeperīmus, neutra alterī officiat
phrases.english: So it will come about that, once we begin to look after both languages with equal care, neither will get in the other’s way.

phrases.latin: vel Mithridātēs, cui duās et vīgintī linguās, quot nātiōnibus imperābat, trāditur nōtās fuisse
phrases.english: or Mithridates, who is said to have known twenty-two languages, one for each nation he ruled
